lead: A weld joins parts by fusing metal, so the joint is permanent and needs no holes. Every weld is sized on the area that actually carries the load, the throat. Once the throat area and the second moments of the weld group are known, an eccentric load splits into a direct part and a moment part, exactly as for a bolt group. Brackets, machine frames, pressure-vessel nozzles and truss gussets are sized this way.
prereq: You need the eccentric bolt-group method of threaded fasteners and bolted joints.

sections.h3: Butt welds, fillet welds and the throat

blocks.text: A butt weld joins plates edge to edge and fills the full thickness (single-V, double-V, U or J edge preparation). Its throat equals the plate thickness t, so under a load P across it σ = P/(tL).

A fillet weld joins two surfaces at a right angle and has a triangular section with leg (size) h. It breaks on its throat, the shortest section through the triangle, at 45°: throat = h cos 45° = 0.707h. A fillet weld is parallel when it runs along the load and transverse when it runs across it.

blocks.where: P is the load one fillet weld carries in N; h the leg in mm; L the effective length in mm (actual length minus about 2h for the craters at start and stop); τ the permissible shear stress in MPa. Two welds carry twice this.

blocks.text: Parallel fillet welds are always checked in shear on the throat. For transverse fillet welds most designers also use shear on the throat; some textbooks use the tensile stress instead (P = 0.707hLσ<sub>t</sub>), so follow your prescribed book. A joint with both kinds is checked as P = 0.707h·ΣL·τ.

sections.h3: Eccentric load in the plane of the welds

blocks.text: When the load lies in the plane of the weld group but misses its centroid G, move it to G and add a torque T = P·e. Treat each weld as a line of zero width (the weld-line method) and multiply by the throat at the end.

items: Find G of the weld lines. For two equal parallel welds it lies midway.
Polar moment J = 0.707h·Σ(L³/12 + L·d²), where d is the distance of each weld's centre from G.
Primary shear τ₁ = P/A, parallel to P and equal everywhere.
Secondary shear τ₂ = T·r/J, square to the line from G, largest at the farthest points.
Add τ₁ and τ₂ as vectors at the corner points: τ = √(τ₁² + τ₂² + 2τ₁τ₂ cos θ). The largest value must not exceed the permissible shear.

sections.h3: Eccentric load causing bending of the welds

blocks.text: A bracket welded to the face of a column, with the load P at distance e from the face, puts the welds in bending about a horizontal axis through G. The load gives a direct shear on the throats and the moment M = P·e gives a bending stress that is largest at the top and bottom of the welds.

blocks.where: A is the throat area in mm²; I the second moment of the throat areas about the bending axis in mm⁴ (two vertical welds of length L: I = 2 × 0.707h·L³/12); y the distance from that axis to the weld end in mm.

blocks.text: The two stresses act at right angles on the throat, so they are combined as a resultant τ = √(σ<sub>b</sub>² + τ₁²), which is the convention of Shigley and Bhandari. Some textbooks use the maximum shear stress instead, ½√(σ<sub>b</sub>² + 4τ₁²); it gives a smaller leg, so state which one you use.
The permissible shear stress comes from the electrode, the code and the inspection level, and examiners state it. Welds under fatigue loading need much lower values, because the weld toe is a notch.

examples.question: Two vertical fillet welds, each with effective length 100 mm and leg h = 6 mm, are 100 mm apart. A vertical load P = 10 kN acts downwards in the plane of the welds, 150 mm to the right of the centroid G. Find the largest resultant shear stress on the throat.
steps: Primary shear: τ₁ = 10 000/848.4 = 11.8 MPa, downwards everywhere.
The weld ends are farthest from G: r = √(50² + 50²) = 70.7 mm, so τ₂ = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 70.7/2.83 × 10⁶ = 37.5 MPa at 45°.
At the ends of the right weld, τ₂ has parts 26.5 MPa across and 26.5 MPa down; with τ₁ the down part is 38.3 MPa, so τ = √(26.5² + 38.3²) = 46.6 MPa.
At the ends of the left weld the down part of τ₂ opposes τ₁: 26.5 − 11.8 = 14.7 MPa, so τ = √(26.5² + 14.7²) = 30.3 MPa.
examples.answer: The largest throat shear is 46.6 MPa, at the top and bottom of the weld nearer the load; the far weld reaches only 30.3 MPa.

examples.question: A bracket plate is welded to a column face by two vertical fillet welds, each 150 mm long, one on each side of the plate. A load P = 15 kN acts downwards 150 mm from the column face. The permissible shear stress in the weld is 80 MPa. Find the leg size h.
steps: Work per mm of leg h. Throat area A = 2 × 0.707h × 150 = 212.1h mm².
Bending stress: σ<sub>b</sub> = 2.25 × 10⁶ × 75/(397 700h) = 424.3/h MPa at the weld ends.
examples.answer: Leg size 6 mm (the maximum shear stress convention would accept 3 mm, so say which convention you use).

traps: Using the leg h as the throat. The throat is 0.707h; using h gives a stress only 0.707 of the true value, an understatement of 29 %.
Adding τ₁ and τ₂ as numbers. They act at an angle: in the first example 11.8 + 37.5 = 49.3 MPa, against the true 46.6 MPa.
Checking only one corner. The weld nearer the load is worse (46.6 MPa) than the far weld (30.3 MPa).
Using J or I of the bracket plate instead of the weld lines times the throat.
Mixing kN·m with mm. Work in N and mm, so stresses come out in MPa.

quiz.q: Why is the throat of an equal-leg fillet weld 0.707h?
quiz.a: The throat is the shortest distance from the root to the face of the 45° triangle: h cos 45° = 0.707h.

quiz.q: Distinguish parallel and transverse fillet welds.
quiz.a: A parallel fillet weld runs along the direction of the load and is loaded in shear along its length. A transverse fillet weld runs across the load.

quiz.q: Why is the primary shear the same everywhere in a weld group while the secondary shear is not?
quiz.a: The direct load is shared equally by the whole throat area. The torque turns the group about G, so the shear grows with the distance r from G.

quiz.q: A fillet weld of leg 8 mm and effective length 150 mm carries 30 kN along its length. Find the throat shear stress.
Two parallel fillet welds, each 80 mm long with leg 5 mm, are 60 mm apart. A 6 kN load parallel to them acts 100 mm from G. Find the largest throat shear.
In the second worked example, why does the bending stress dominate the direct shear?
quiz.a: σ<sub>b</sub>/τ₁ = (M·y/I)/(P/A) = 6e/L for these welds = 6 × 150/150 = 6. Any lever arm comparable with the weld length makes bending about six times the direct shear, so longer welds help more than a larger leg.

beyond: Not for the exam. Welded structures are designed to codes such as IS 800 and AWS D1.1, which fix permissible stresses by electrode and inspection level. Fatigue of welded joints is checked with detail categories (S–N curves for each weld shape), because the weld toe is a sharp notch with residual stress. Search for weld detail category, weld toe grinding and hot-spot stress.

figure.caption: The worked example’s two 100 mm fillet welds, 100 mm apart, with the 10 kN load 150 mm from G. At the ends of the right weld the primary shear τ₁ (11.8 MPa) and the torsional shear τ₂ (37.5 MPa) add to 46.6 MPa; the left weld’s ends reach only 30.3 MPa.
